definition: Vigorous means full of energy, force, or strength.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word vigorous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know vigorous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Two hours in, the town-hall debate stayed vigorous, hands still shooting up faster than the moderator could point.
A mild workout barely raises your pulse; vigorous action puts real force and strength behind every motion.
Lively means brisk and animated; vigorous adds muscle - a lively conversation sparkles, while a vigorous one is a full-contact sport.

Energetic says a person or action is full of active energy — always in motion, never idle. Vigorous adds force and strength to that energy: a vigorous scrub bears down, a vigorous debate pushes hard. An energetic child circles the yard all afternoon; a vigorous one wins the tug-of-war.

Spirited points at verve — the flash of personality and heart inside an effort, like a spirited reply or a spirited pony. Vigorous measures the muscle behind the action rather than the personality in it. A spirited defense has heart; a vigorous defense has force.

Dynamic describes energy that drives change and keeps things moving — a dynamic speaker, a dynamic young company. Vigorous names the raw force and strength inside the action itself, whether or not anything changes. A dynamic firm keeps reinventing itself; a vigorous one simply outworks its rivals.

Vigorous describes the doer, not the task: it names energy, force, and strength in the action itself.
A vigorous effort attacks the work; whether the work is hard is a separate question.
Vigorous praises the force in an action or person - exercise, debate, growth, scrubbing.
Keep it apart from its unit-mate strenuous, which measures what a task demands rather than what a person brings: the workout is strenuous, the athlete is vigorous.
For personality rather than force, lively or spirited is the lighter touch.

For sixty years the boathouse's dawn crew has included at least one member over eighty.
Visitors expect to find the elders paddling gently at the back of the boat; instead they set the pace.
Their strokes stay vigorous - full pulls that bend the oars and drive real force into the water - while younger rowers often coast between bursts.
A sports physiologist who filmed the crew found the seniors applying more power per stroke, not merely taking more strokes.
Her conclusion ran against the club's folklore: what fades with age is not strength itself but the willingness to spend it.
